Title: LSJ - How can this be right

Messages.Author: martin.c...@southbeds.gov.uk
Messages.Body:
I participated in my first competitive game of VTES in about 3 and
half years or so at the weekend. The UK Nationals as it happened. I
qualified for the final, played as well as I could (in light of the
fact I knew none of the new cards and could only remember how to play
'about well enough') but got screwed over so I ended up third.

All the way through the preliminary rounds it was drummed into me that
there's a play to win rule now - you've gotta be prey focussed, and
can get pulled up by the judge if they think you are taking a move
which isn't in the interest of you nabbing a VP.

And yet, in the final, a deal was struck where someone agreed to come
SECOND, help another player oust me (who would therefore take first)
and then roll over.

Where's the playing to win here? Why do you not have to play to win
in a final? Can I really play for 2nd place if I fancy the prize more
than what's on offer for first? Or worse still, can I just back oust
someone, then transfer myself out, because a good mate of mine is my
grand-predator and I'd really like him to win?

If this is the state of competitive VTES play now, I'm bloody glad I'm
out of it.

Marty
Super pissed about the turn of events

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1191829130.0...@d55g2000hsg.googlegroups.com>,

martin.c...@southbeds.gov.uk writes:
>All the way through the preliminary rounds it was drummed into me that
>there's a play to win rule now - you've gotta be prey focussed, and
>can get pulled up by the judge if they think you are taking a move
>which isn't in the interest of you nabbing a VP.

You have to play to win, but you do not have to play to nab every VP.

For example, you can back oust a player or cross-table oust a player,
and that doesn't violate Play to Win if it's in your interests. For
example, you're in a choice between oust your prey or back oust your
predator. If you get your prey, you'll go back up to 7 or 8 pool, but
then your predator will stealth-bleed you out. So you can happily pass
up the VP to back-oust your predator. There are many other situations
like this. If the judge believes that you're still trying to play to
get the Game Win, it's likely to be legitimate Play to Win[0] play.

Additionally, it is absolutely not the judge's responsibility to correct
poor play. As anyone who's ever watched a tense game of V:TES knows,
there are tons of times when you see someone make a mistake that loses
them the game. The judge is not supposed to correct poor play, if it's
actually poor play.

That is, you must always play for a table win, however it's available.
If there are several ways of getting a table win (a 3-2 split, a 5-0
sweep), pick whichever you want. You cannot give up the game win and
come second, but the judge cannot disallow a move just because it stops
you getting a particular VP.

Then if you're not able to get a table win, you play to get as many VPs
as possible.

>And yet, in the final, a deal was struck where someone agreed to come
>SECOND, help another player oust me (who would therefore take first)
>and then roll over.
>
>Where's the playing to win here? Why do you not have to play to win
>in a final? Can I really play for 2nd place if I fancy the prize more
>than what's on offer for first?

Yes.

Devil's advocate: Would you be happy coming away from a tournament with
a prize you didn't want, when you could have got the one you really
wanted?

However, for this reason, it is a bad idea to have prizes specifically
allocated to places (other than, say, a small trophy for first place).
Have prizes, let players pick. Two rare pieces of artwork and a booster
box? Let the first three players pick which they want. Player in first
place doesn't give a stuff about art? He walks off with a box of
boosters instead. Organizer doesn't think that's appropriate for first
place, who must get something "better"? Organizer gets over himself.

>Or worse still, can I just back oust
>someone, then transfer myself out, because a good mate of mine is my
>grand-predator and I'd really like him to win?

That would potentially violate either the Sportsmanship or, potentially,
Collusion clauses of the rules.

Players in the final are assumed to be playing to win, but that doesn't
mean that all actions are therefore legal.

[0] That's not to say that *every* piece of behaviour that will lead to
a Game Win is legal. Some of it might be collusion with another player,
say, or illegal somehow in some other way.

--
James Coupe

The answer to your question is simple. In any vtes game not everyone
is in a position to win. Most of the time it is only 1 or 2 depending
on the development of the game. However, some people can optimise the
amount of victory points by making a deal.

Furthermore, to be prey focused is not necessarily the way to play the
game. say you play weenie pander and your small prey is a weenie
auspex, you might chill on your prey for him to take on VP before you
kill him.

In general, the aim is to gain the maximum points out of a given
situation, someitmes if this means giving the table to someone else,
so be it.

Ruben

Playing to win means this:

1) You have to strive to get a gamewin.
2) If you do not have a reasonable chance to get a gamewin, you have
to strive to maximize the amount of VPs you get.
3) If you do not have a reasonable chance to get another VP , you are
free to do whatever you want (lose as you choose).

So, if this player was in situation 3, and could get more prizes from
playing one way or the other, that's his full right.

Sucks to be you! :P

Cheers,
B

martin.c...@southbeds.gov.uk wrote:
> I participated in my first competitive game of VTES in about 3 and
> half years or so at the weekend. The UK Nationals as it happened. I
> qualified for the final, played as well as I could (in light of the

> 'about well enough') but got screwed over so I ended up third.
>
> All the way through the preliminary rounds it was drummed into me that
> there's a play to win rule now - you've gotta be prey focussed, and

Well, there's always been a play to win rule (it's part of "sportsmanship"), but
yes, there is one now still.

You don't have to be prey-focussed. You simply play to win. If PTW involves
focus on your prey, fine. If not, fine.

> can get pulled up by the judge if they think you are taking a move
> which isn't in the interest of you nabbing a VP.

Well, if the activity is counter to the interest of PTW.

> And yet, in the final, a deal was struck where someone agreed to come
> SECOND, help another player oust me (who would therefore take first)
> and then roll over.
>

> Where's the playing to win here?

Apparently the play couldn't come in first himself.
So second, being the best he can do, is PTW.

> Why do you not have to play to win
> in a final?

Well, why wouldn't you play for the best finish you can?

In preliminaries, there are future game considerations. In the final, there are
none such. So, barring collusion or other in-itself illegal activity, all
activity in a final can be assumed to be PTW, since the player has no other
conflicting considerations.

> Can I really play for 2nd place if I fancy the prize more
> than what's on offer for first?

The default state of affairs is for first place prize to be a strict superset of
any other.

> Or worse still, can I just back oust
> someone, then transfer myself out, because a good mate of mine is my
> grand-predator and I'd really like him to win?

No. That would be unsportmanlike (possibly collusion).

On Oct 8, 11:27 am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

> Apparently the play couldn't come in first himself.
> So second, being the best he can do, is PTW.

Two points. Firstly, this player had two avenues for 2nd place:
1. To oust his prey with my help, then 'roll' to me
2. To help is prey oust me, then 'roll' to him.
The fact that both of these two would have netted him the same
positioning means that other factors then come into it.

>
> Well, why wouldn't you play for the best finish you can?

Well, that really is the question isn't it. Making a deal to place
2nd is hardly 'the best you can'. The best any of us 3 could have
finished was first. Simple as that. We all had pool, we all had
minions, we all had ways to oust our prey. There are so many factors
that simply weren't considered. As previously stated, I had Gabrin
out that could have been used to tap younger vamps - ie. all of my
predators. I had a sensory dep, and the stealth to push it through.
I had little forward pressure in my hand, but a lot of defensive
tricks. All of this adds up to my predator being up against it, and
my prey probably being able to force his way through and gain another
VP that way. And they it comes down to a one on one between me and
him. Again, a battle that could have gone either way.

In short, I don't believe he was playing to win.

Messages.Author: Salem
Messages.Body:


As far as I understand it, the judge just has to believe that the
*player* is reasonably sure they cannot advance their position. That
player is not allowed to look at your hand, and is also not required to
believe anything you might say about your hand or what plays you might make.

It leaves a god-awful taste in the mouth, and can generate some nasty
ill-will when it happens. But at the end of the day, isn't it just a
game? (I'm not saying don't vent, and don't just sit back and accept the
way the rules are. I do believe most people would love to hear
suggestions about how to minimise king-making, and try and reign
deal-making back into more 'acceptable' levels).

But as has been shown countless times, just saying 'the rules suck'
doesn't help much for the establishment of better rules. There needs to
be options.

Like that Nystulc person. They're trying, and they're thinking. Which is
all good. And it's stimulating healthy debate (and it's taken an
amazingly long time for the thread to get flamey, I am so proud of
everyone!). I don't agree with much of what Nystulc is saying, but that
doesn't mean what they're saying isn't right, or at the least isn't
worth thinking about.



Messages.Author: mgre...@googlemail.com
Messages.Body:
A kingmaking deal:
A deal whereby the actions of one player will result in him
determining the outcome of a tournament.

A coin flip:
In such a situation a judge flips a coin to see which of the two
potential kings wins.

Rather than get caught up in a hail of rebuffs as to how this can be
played around: what about at least giving this as an option? In the
case in point Antonio can't win and neither can Ant without Antonio's
help. Antonio offers help to Ant.

The judge identifies this as a potential kingmaking deal and offers
Martin a choice:

1) Let the deal stand: he takes on the pair of them.
2) Let a coin flip decide the winner (Ant or Martin).

It seems to me to be a shade more elegant than letting OoG
considerations determine an outcome.

Thoughts?

GreenO

Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:
On Oct 8, 6:05 am, martin.cubber...@southbeds.gov.uk wrote:
> On Oct 8, 2:03 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
>
> > > EVERYONE else that was at the tournment, including the guy that won,
> > > see's this as an issue.
>
> > Issues are all well and good. Solutions are better.
>
> No point offering solutions until you acknowledge there's a problem.
> Do this, and we can all discuss how this can be avoided in the future.

Kingmaking is part of many--if not most--multiplayer games. As is
"gang up on the leader", and so on. Garfield created the pred/prey
relationship and the VP only for ousting prey to *reduce* the amount
of kingmaking possible. He never tried to create a game where
kingmaking was illegal or impossible. I'm not sure it is worth arguing
over whether this requires the tag "problem". It simply is an aspect
of this and many other multiplayer games.

That said, I'm sure most people would love to see VTES have a little
less ability for king-making and less opportunity for players to
quickly fold in a final and play for 2nd place.

If someone has some good suggestions for how to reduce king-making and
further encourage players to win the current game (finals included),
I'd love to hear them.

Past suggestions have been about flat prize distribution & flat rating
points & flat finishes (one player wins and the rest are tied for 2nd--
this does nothing for reducing king-making but it does reduce the
motivation to folding for someone to earn 2nd place).

-Robert

Ok, first make note that I'm only giving my humble opinion.
I think that the problem with finals in this game is just a problem of
prize giving, probably because a multiplayer game needs a change in
thoughts about prize givings.
See, in 1 vs.1 games, it stands to logic that the person ending second
should get a better prize than the person ending third, just because
most times the second player beated third, or a person who has played
and beated third.
But the same does not hold true when the game has 5 people playing, as
it encourages people make "losing" deals just to end, losing, in a
better position than the other players.

second to fifth, the people in the final not ending first, should be
the same, so in the end, if you haven't won, it doesn't matter if you
end second or fifth.

It sounds very much to me like Antonio was in a very bad position and
made as much of it as he thought was possible. Just to make sure I'm
clear on what happened, I'll go through this. If I get anything wrong,
please correct me.

Antonio's minions were weak, he had 6 bleed cards and a misdirection,
and Anthony had enough untapped minions to block every action, or
every action but 1 if he played misdirection. He might be able to get
a single bleed through this turn if he plays misdirection on his prey,
and his prey has no deflections or wakes. If he does this, he is
tapped out. Martin has 5 bleed to Antonio's 7 pool, without playing
any cards.

He can go all out forward and hope that Martin does not oust him next
turn for some reason. He can do nothing this turn and hope that his
options are somehow better next turn. Without some kind of deal, his
situation looks pretty close to hopeless.

Once Antonio decides to attempt a deal, he can deal with his prey or
his predator. If he deals with his predator (Martin), he may be able
to gain 1 VP and 6 pool. He has to convince his Martin to Sense Dep
and Gabrin-tap Anthony's minions (and he can't be sure that Sense Dep
is even in Martin's hand). Unfortunately, Antonio doesn't have much to
offer to entice Martin into this deal - he essentially has to credibly
threaten to gang with Anthony. Also unfortunately, Antonio has no way
to ensure that Martin will live up to his end of the deal, or survive
if Martin decides to break it. Anthony might even be able to backoust
him if he deals with Martin. Antonio can also not guarantee that his
placement will end up better than 2nd even if he does get one
additional VP by ousting Anthony with Martin's help. He gains 6 pool,
which helps, but his minions are still weak and he will spend most or
all of their blood by bleeding Anthony. If Martin breaks the deal,
Anthony could fall into 3rd place.

Instead, Antonio offers a deal to Anthony, to oust Martin and secure
2nd place with near certainty. There is no incentive for Anthony to
decline or break the deal, and no incentive for Anthony not to take
the deal. It's as close to a guaranteed 2nd place finish as you can
get. Without having been there or reading anyone's mind, it's possible
that Antonio may have even been trying to prompt Martin to make the
counteroffer, but he can't take a deal that's not offered.

Given that, I don't think it's reasonable to say that Antonio made his
decision based on where that piece of artwork was going, though it
still would have been a better idea to let (make?) Anthony keep his
artwork if he won the tournament (he could then offer it as prize at
the next tournament if he really wanted to).

witness1

True enough,
I do not understand your reaction, Marty... I want to formulate it.
Your are in a situation where your predator has the need of only 3
cards to kill you in the next turn: 2 bleed modifiers and 1 stealth
card. You have a total hand jam and you cannot cycle because you will
be blocked by your prey and one more vampire will be tapped.

What is the best solution is, if nobody offers you anything?
Your best solution is to ally with your prey for much reasons:
- free cycling of your hand. By bleeding and being bounced, you might
draw deflections that allow you to survive next turn. Eventually, your
bleeds might be bounced back by your predator and you might eventually
find an opportunity to kill your prey.
- pression on your predator. If he doesn't have all the cards to kill
you, he might likely have a much more defensive behaviour next turn
(if he is still alive). A sensory deprivation that could have been
intended to be kept for the 2-players final dual might be used before
than expected
-if your predator dies, you secure the second seat. If your prey gets
troubles on her way (because of combat damages or whatever) then you
might play for first.

The other solutions:
- waiting doesn't bring you anything. With 6 bleed cards, your hand is
not likely to change. Your predator has already 4 bleed points out
- asking your predator to let you kill your prey. You know it is not
possible because of your hand and you also know that a counter-deal
will be: your prey tells your predator that he can kill you and your
predator will accept because it allows him to be first or second
depending on the final dual. The counter-deal could eventually be
immediately offered and you could already be dead when you make the
deal.

Then Antonio's choice was wise. This is insulting him to suggest he
might have played to collude. He played his best for play to win. I
don't know how he feels right now but I feel very bad for him, knowing
him as I do, to be the center of all those problematics when all he
did was to abide by the rules and get a wonderful second place. Yes,
being second is already

In message <1191849931.3...@50g2000hsm.googlegroups.com>,
mgre...@googlemail.com writes:
>A kingmaking deal:
>A deal whereby the actions of one player will result in him
>determining the outcome of a tournament.

During the execution of a kingmaking deal, it is not impossible for the
kingmaker to end up in a better position - because the predator he dealt
with isn't bleeding him, for example.

In such a situation, the kingmaker may be able to viably get back on his
feet, and fight it out to get the win instead of second place, but will
never be able to do that without the king-making deal. e.g. a deck that
can now amass a bit of pool with a few pool-gain actions, when it's not
having to fend off another deck so much.

Carefully played, some apparently king-making deals can lead to the
opportunity for back-stabbing and deal-breaking. A coin flip loses
that.

> seems to me to be both novel and important. Is this ruling really
> correct? If so, it seems to me that it completely moots the rule that
> all deals are off when the table is reduced to two players.

Good point, IMO. From what I read on this thread, I'm inclined to
believe that conceding the game was legal at that point (so there is
not necessarily a conflict with the "all deals are void when the game
is reduced to players" rule). But, when there are only two players
left, is there a good reason for not playing for whatever small chance
you still have to beat the other player? (Unless, maybe, the other
player already has the GW and you have already guaranteed second place
on tie-breakers).

> Beyond the rules mooting issue, it also seems to me that it sucks.
> The clear intention of the rule is that the remaining two players
> should play to win the game. I don't see any way to _not_ violate
> Play to Win by conceding when either player could still earn enough
> VPs for a Game Win.

Agreed.

> What would it hurt to actually play it out?

We would have to be there to know better. But I have ruled earlier
this year that two players should play out a table both were about to
give up on (a deadlock was by far the most likely outcome at that
point).

The problem with their decision was that both still had a shot at the
GW, unlikely as it was. (Incidentally, the GW would get the winner a
5th seed to the final table of a continental qualifier, a situation
they weren't aware of. This bit isn't important, though, as it would
be an out-of-table consideration, and thus immaterial to judge the
validity of their "deal").

The bottom line was that I was not sure whether or not I should tell
them to play it out, or let them give up on the basis that it was not
illegal play, just poor(ish) play.

I still think I could have ruled either way as far as the rules go,
but I thought that playing things out and trying to win is usually the
best decision - and the best outcome to a good game.

> If Antonio was really in a lost position, it shouldn't take long. If
> not, well, then he can't concede under play to win, right? And if he
> won't play to win, then he is disqualified and another player can play
> out his position, or whatever.

As I said before, I believe that his conceding was probably legal -
because it all boils down to whether or not he still had a chance to
win (even the tiniest one). More to the point, whether or not he
believed he had a chance.

Still, it's head to head, so I'd probably like to see this one played
to the very end if I were the judge (and by no means this is meant as
a criticism to Damnans or the other judges involved, I'm just throwing
my personal view on this specific kind of situation).

Messages.Author: Clément
Messages.Body:
On Oct 9, 6:13 am, Martin.Cubber... wrote:

> On Oct 8, 8:45 pm, Blooded Sand wrote:
>
> > You miss what my point is. Playing for anything but first place, no
> > matter how slim the chance, is in my opinion chickening out.
> > Especially in a final.
> > Play. To. Win.
> > Not to come second/third/fourth/fifth. Win.

See, that's when things get mixed up a little bit. It's totally
possible to play for second place (or third, or fourth, or fifth) and
still be playing to win. All it takes for this to be true is that
whatever position you are aiming at is the best position you can
reasonably expect to achieve. As has been pointed out before, many
times.

(...)

>
> > When you have no minions left, little pool and no resources, then
> > you've lost. Till then you can keep on trying.
>
> That is entirely my feeling on the matter mate - though I'm beginning
> to think it's playstyle or a 'personal interpretation' of what play to
> win means, rather than anything else.

"Playstile", yes. "Personal interpretation" of play to win, not quite.
Play to win should always be interpreted as defined by the rules.

> Some people like the above (you
> and other), others are happy to secure a 2nd place rather than take a
> risk at 1st. I'm happy to say I'll never be in the latter camp.

It's worth noting that, as a player, I fully agree with both of you.
I'm always glad to risk a 2nd seed position and go for the tournament
win, even if it means that I might end up fifth.

But that doesn't mean I don't think that assuring the best position
you can possibly get isn't a solid goal. Because it is. And it's
perfectly in the spirit of playing the game.

Finishing second is better than finishing third, in at least a couple
of levels (tournament table and ratings). And there is not anything
intrinsically wrong with that.

If a player is not aiming at a better position because he is afraid of
taking risks, or because his assessment of the table state is poor,
then it's the player's fault (disclaimer: I'm not talking about
Antonio here - from what I read here, his decision might have been the
best one he could make).

If a player is not aiming at a better position because he is
colluding, for example, then it's illegal play.

Other than poor play and illegal play, I fail to see where aiming at
the best position you can possibly achieve is something bad, even if
that position is not 1st anymore.

Abraço,

Luiz Mello

> minions' or 'knock you down to one pool and oops I ousted you'

I think the trick here is to remove the blanket assumption that, just
by virtue of having your ass in a chair at the final table, everything
and anything you do is "play to win." Then judges can adequately
leverage the existing PtW rule. IMO there is more abuse of PtW in the
finals, as people whore out reflexively for 2nd place etc than in the
prelims. In the prelims people have a natural motivator to play to
win: they want to make the finals. In the finals there is no such
natural motivator, and with flawed rules like the PtW assumption and
the legality of prize support splits, there is even some incentive
against it.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
bluedevil wrote:
> On Oct 8, 8:06 am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
>
>> OK, then. Without any indication of illegal activity, then the actions of the
>> finalists can be assumed to be PTW, since there is no other competing consideration.
>
> You have asserted this many times in the past. It seems to me that
> there are no practical grounds for assuming it.

Only the grounds that players are humans.

> There is evidence to the contrary: there are less natural incentives
> to strive for GW's and VP's than in the preliminary rounds when
> everyone is trying to make the finals.

How so?

In the prelims, the tournament structure itself could occasionally compete
(someone wanting to take fewer VPs xerself in order to swing a GW from one
opponent to another because that swing helps isolate/spread the GWs in a manner
that raises/secures the player's own standing).

In the final, there is no future consideration to compete with the final game
itself.

If you discount the reality of the tournament structure, you could make the case
that the two were equal in natural incentives, perhaps. But not the case that
the final has fewer natural incentives. Which incentives do the prelims have
that the final does not?

Winning rewarded most? check.
VPs rewarded next most? check.

> If this assumption were to be repealed, wouldn't it give judges a
> freer hand, the same degree of freedom they have in the prelims, to
> judge whether a VP deal is PtW? What harm is done in bringing things
> back into parity?

They are in parity. If a player is actively not playing to win, then the judge
is free to identify the reason the player is not playing to win (the "other
illegal activity" that leads to the player actively playing against xer own best
interests) and correct the situation.

The bit about assuming the players are playing to win in the finals barring
other illegal activity is just a restatement of the reality that there is no
competing consideration in the final, as there (infrequently) could be in the
prelims.

Howdy,

> > > > I would much rather this, yes. Throw the line, and have a 'you're
> > > > alive, you play for 1st' rule in effect.
>
> > > Nice sound bite.
>
> > > Horrid in practice.
>
> > Why's that?
>
> Example: My prey has just scored 2 VPs. He is coming close to scoring
> a third VP by ousting my predator. Under your proposition, I MUST do
> everything in my power to stop my prey from ousting a third player
> (since that gives him an automatic game win, and loss for me) even if
> there is a ridiculously high (but less than 100%) chance that my
> predator will oust me after I spend the resources on this. I am not
> allowed to conserve resources and attempt to oust him for 2 VPs in the
> 1-on-1 game, even if my chances of doing this are much better than
> getting the game win.

It sounds to me like the finals scoring system Martin is suggesting is
effectively 'winner take all'. In such a system, the game would end
at the point that one player got 3 VP, so, yes, it would be entirely
pointless to play for 2 VPs in the endgame.

I'm sure there must also be issues with 'winner take all', but the
above issue isn't one of them. You definitely go all out to stop
someone else from winning, as, once they have, you can't. Of course,
there would be consequences for prize support, ranking, etc. Final
tables would be scored 'winner' + 'also ran'.

Alex

The judge is not predicting the outcome of the game, as I understand
it the judge is expected to judge wether the player making the deal
*feels* that *they* have no chance to win the game. As the player
making
the deal does not know the contents of opponenets hands, the judge
should not base an evaluation of the deal on the opponents' hands.
Ash heaps, cards in play - yes, hand - no, not withstanding various
cards
that show persons hands to the participants.

This opens all sorts of pandora's boxes, as sometimes players are to
dense to see a way out and such, but its the best we got right now.

This next bit I think you stumbled across while you were typing but
just in case...
As to why evaluating hands is a bad idea, where does it stop? In
evaluating
a particular player's hand, they only need evaluate "is it reasonable
that this
player considers their current position hopeless" ie not going to gain
further VPs.

Its not an easy evaluation, but its usually not impossible.

If you add evaluation of other players hands then the judge must
speculate that
these other players will assist, or not assist. "Hmmm... he's got a
Sens Dep.
but that guy over there has a DI, I wonder if he would use it on the
Sense Dep?"
There quickly become too many possibilities for any judge to
evaluate,
and this is further increased by the fact that players do not always
play logically
or consistently. Person X having a Sens Dep does not neccessarily mean
it
would be used one way or another, and the last thing tournaments need
is the judge having to pull each finalist aside to have a discussion
about how they
plan to use the cards in their hand at this point in time.

>From a practicality standpoint, the judge must evaluate on the same
perspective
that the player making the deal has.

"No you can't make that deal, you've still got a shot, but I can't
tell you why.
However I do feel that you should look at that guy over there and
flatter him
somewhat so that if he hypothetically can help you he might then be
inclined to
do so". Nudge nudge wink wink.
Kinda hoses the other players who may have been relying on surprise.

I don't like vp deals in the finals or even in the prelims.
I think it sucks the life out of playgroups as people get turned off
by them.
I think the assumption of PTW in the finals is flawed as humans are
essentially flawed but I got nothing better from a practical
standpoint.

Where does the two-man exception in 4.8 of the VEKN rules come in?
"when only two Methuselahs remain, the tournament rules no longer
acknowledge any deals. Prior deals are voided, even if they were play
to win when made. When only two Methuselahs remain, both
Methuselahs must play to win based only on game state, without
regard to any deals."

In the described situation where one player "rolled over" to the
eventual winner, did this not violate the quoted exception? I guess
it boils down to how they went about "rolling over".

John P.

about rulings, trying to convince him of their point of view.

of arguements that he faces at a tournament. It
would gain him nothing. If people are willing to argue with
the current highest authority of rules, no judge certification
process will cause fewer arguements for other people.
Because there are always people who will argue (some
politely, some less so) with a judgement.

to listen.

suddenly be unsanctioned tournaments here. This discussion
about the validity of a test is less than worthless until
such a test is created and we both know what the other
expects.

There would need to be a penalty outlined for failing
the tests, probably an appeals process where reasons
can be explained and considered. Nothing is really
black and white in this game except really simple
questions like can you play a conditioning with
a bonding, and that type of test will not prove anything.

the deck chairs on the Titanic.

National event become invalid? Is that what you want for VTES?

> Unless you're a judge yourself and you don't like the idea to endure some

I judge the local tournaments and have for the last five years. My
players
are very web savy and check their own rulings from time to time. So I
spend
a fair amount of time keeping up to date. But not everyone has the
time
to do this.

I will take any test required of me, but there is a large unheard
population
out there that does not have the time that I do to monitor this
newsgroup.
Those potential judges should not be penalized for doing the best they
can for their players.

The
tournament organizers pick judges that they believe to be good. This
is a better measure of quality judging than any test you or I could
come
up with. Hugh (whom I believe organized the UK nationals) decided
who would be the judges at this event. As Hugh is probably one of the
most
well travelled VTES players I have met I would respect his choices.

The sitation appears to be more that some players did not
understand the play to win rules as they currently stand. I
base this on the ongoing discussions in this thread
between players and LSJ.

But the fact of the matter appears to be that Gines rules in
accordance with the Play to Win rules. If Gines made the correct
call based on the current rules then yay Gines. It would be nice if
all the judges were on the same page.

I think it would have to be a very exhaustive testing procedure
to screen out the finer nuances of "Play to Win" alone,
let alone cover the breadth of VTES rulings in the last 13 years.
Consistency good.
Exhaustive testing procedure to get it... not so good.

> I'd say that a certified judge should show a good understanding of the
> fundamentals (easy enough) and be provided with a set of learning
> examples as to how to rule under various circumstances. Its more for me
> about a learning process that produces consistent judging from one judge
> to another, than it is taking a test for "stinking badges"... I'm
> personaly not even interested a certification process, per se, as I am a
> consistent basis for training the judging of things such as PTW, deal
> legality, etc. The "use _your_ judgement" model needs be discarded at
> some point, and be replaced with a "use _this_ judgement" model, instead.

I would rather see the rules made more clear so that judges
could more easily understand such things than create models
to try and understand them. Examples are always good, but
anybody who can google can get examples now.

> Robert Goudie <RobertT.Gou...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> If someone has some good suggestions for how to reduce
>> king-making and further encourage players to win the
>> current game (finals included), I'd love to hear them.
>
> I'm also reminded of the unfinished discussion w/ Kevin (reading this
> Kevin?) when he asserted he didn't want different time limits because
> the final round should be exactly the same as the prelim rounds. I
> wish I would have thought about the PtW aberration when we were
> discussing this. An additional path to victory by timing out as top
> seed, and no practical Play to Win rule. Yep, sounds like the same
> game to me.

Well, in contract to this so-called "everyone is assumed to be playing to
win, since it is the finals" theory, I believe, rather, that there really
ISN'T a PTW rule in the finals, since if you are in 5th place, you are
allowed to behave in any ridiculously foolish fashion you want --
including self-ousting to determine the winner -- and since it isn't
causing you to lose any standing, it isn't, and can't be, penalized.

Personally, I would suggest a few changes to the VTES finals:
a. Make the finals have only one "winner", and the rest are "runners-up".
b. Make the finals have the same time limit as the prelimimary rounds.
c. Either allow ANY play for ANY or NO REASON WHATSOEVER (i.e. consistent
with current judging methodology, despite the "everyone is assumed to be
playing-to-win" red herring) **OR** disallow SOME play (e.g. self-ousting,
dubious deals) in order to PRESERVE so-called PLAY TO WIN theory.

If you think I have not pointed out the drawbacks of testing then you
have not been understanding what I have been saying (Or you don't
believe what I am saying).

The drawbacks of a test:
1) Administering the test. Yeah the test can be automated but there's
work involved in deciding what should be included, what level of
knowledge is expected, making sure judges are tested frequently
enough. This can't be taken lightly as presumably your tests are going
to have consequences.
2) Penalties. If you're testing there have to be penalties (or why
have a test?). Likely not letting that person judge would be a
penalty. This means that an even can get screwed over when a judge
suddenly gets "DQed". As soon as someone can't judge then there's
going to be endless arguements about the applicability of said test.
Is there an appeals process?
3) Barrier to entry. VTES needs new players and new play groups. This
means that in cities where no one has played before, its advantagous
to new players to be able to sign someone up to judge and actually
have organized play. Yeah sure there might be mistakes for a while,
but at that level it is not going to hurt anyone. If you tell a new
player stuggling to get a tournament scene started that they have to
pass a test before running an event, unless that test is simple in the
extreme (ie worthless) some of those new players will not make it. We
want every possibly player who expresses an interest in VTES organized
play to be able to play. Barriers to entry, no matter how small are
BAD.
4) People make errors. Testing will not eliminate errors caused by
exhaustion, irritation, or stress. They MIGHT reduce errors caused by
ignorance, but I'm thinking more errors in judging are not from
ignorance, but from other factors. If a test cannot eliminate what I
think is the most common cause of judging errors, than testing is not
worthwhile, and testing is then a bad idea.

There's a whole slew of issues that have to be worked out prior to any
testing being considered. Until you propose a test, create a sample
test to give us the idea of scope and depth, lay out penalities, etc
for the test, figure out all of the logistics and consequences, you
have not done sufficient work to justify proposing a test. And if your
response is "I didn't mean I should write a test" then do not even
bother replying. Write up a sample test or a small portion of a sample
test. Tell us what you would expect from such a test. (I'm not saying
program it, but just sample questions). Determine what is a "pass",
what are the consequences of not passing, how often would someone need
to be tested. Maybe it will be brilliant and I will become a proponent
of testing, but I do not see it happening for the resons I've outlined
above. I will not continue to argue about testing (other than to say
it is bad) until you provide more details about what you think testing
encompasses.

> Google search is a pain, mostly, we know that.
> You can't simply have rulings scattered here and there, and this is another
> issue that should be adressed, speaking of rules consistency.

Unified is nice, keeping it up to date and determining if every new
question needs to go into the unified rulings is more pain. Scott does
archive rulings on a yahoo group somewhere. (I get the emails, I just

First, bad play is not illegal. If the judge spots a path to victory
that the player does not, I'm not in favor of the judge pointing that
out.

Finalists are assumed to be playing to win unless you have reason to
believe there's some consideration outside of the current game that's
interfering with the goal of playing to win. It could be "I suspect
this guy's sacrificing his standing to point out some flaw in the
rules" or "this guy is rolling a die and bleeding randomly crosstable
based on the results" or anything else. The only difference is that in
the preliminary rounds, there are considerations that are out-of-game,
but not out-of-tournament (like "I don't want to see deck Y in the
finals"). So the "assumption" is merely pointing out that these
considerations no longer exist in the finals.

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:


I imagine this point has been brought up in some variation, but I
haven't read all 300+ posts in this thread.

In the preliminaries, every additional VP or GW has an incremental
bonus associated with it: You can earn a higher ranking going into the
final. Therefore, there are significant advantages for playing for
every VP possible, even once you have secured a GW with 3 VPs.

However, once you're at the final table, all you have to do to "win"
is be better than everyone else under time constraints. If the table
times out, the #1 seed wins. If you earn 1 VP and the table times out,
you win.

These possibilities warp play style at the final table in many
instances and this is really what people are complaining about and
want changed. The "play until someone has 3 VPs then stop" idea has
some merit, but only insofar as determining a winner is concerned.
It's fairly unsatisfying when a game ends without coming to its full
conclusion. One could argue that VTES would become a race to 3 VPs
which is something the game win rule was designed to mitigate.

So, one bonus VP for Last Man Standing in all games, and results from
finals are determined independently from standings going into
finals. ;)

Jeff

2.2. Tournament Organizer Responsibilities

The tournament organizer for an event is ultimately responsible for
all tournament operations and event reporting for the event. The
tournament organizer's responsibilities include, but are not limited
to, the following:

* Selecting the site for the event
* Providing all materials to operate the event (product at Sealed
Deck events, and so on)

an appropriate head judge for the event)

date

responsibilities.

It is. And for rulings on how various cards interact with each other and
the rules, "mechanically" if you will, its sufficient and excellent.

Its the cases where a judge, using his judgment, must decide if a
course of action for a player is PTW, or not, or if a deal is legal, that
we are getting the judging inconsistency that I poorly alluded to, above.
Take the example from this thread;

Damnans, using his judgment, assessed the game state and Antonio's
proposed deal, and ruled it to be legal, as it was maximizing his
outcome.

Rob, using his judgment, asessed the game state and Antonio's proposed
deal, and assessed it to be illegal, as it was not maximizing his outcome
(but kept this observation to himself, as he was not the current head
judge).

Under the rules as they stand, with each "judge using his judgment", both
of them ruled correctly. Were Gines' and Rob's roles reversed, then
Rob's ruling would be the one which the rules (and LSJ) would uphold,
because the rules hold the judge's judgment as inerrant with respect to
the Judge's assessment of the game state, regardless of what that
assessment may be. At least for the purposes of training judges, a
single correct assessment of the game state should be strived for, so in
that respect, Google searches are a poor tool to train with...

Messages.Author: illarion
Messages.Body:
> Correct. Obviously if the rules are changed to flatten the final rewards to just
> two tiers ("winner" and "other finalist"), then the rule on splitting prizes
> would be changed as well.

With all due respect to those suggesting final standing be changed to
"1st vs runners up", I think this is a terrible idea. It simply
doesn't reflect fairly the accomplishments of the runners up -
especially the potential poor sap who got 2vp. Surely he has played
better, done better in achieving his goals, than the three players who
got 0vp?
Personally, I find this "If you don't win, you lose" attitude
baffling. Sure, I play for first, and many times I've traded a safe
2nd for a shot at first - but I don't consider 2nd place in a major
tournament to be unworthy of note! (Perhaps this is simply because
I've only won a few major tournaments, unlike some of the more
illustrious players here :) ).

Many don't care about this, but thematically I find it satisfying
also. We are supposed to be ancient vampires, subtly working against
one another to increase our power and influence - NOT to eradicate ALL
the others and be last man standing. Gaining a VP or two and
withdrawing from the struggle would be far more in character.
(I'm not suggesting that making withdrawal easier or more rewarding
would be good for the game, mind).

> IT WASN'T THE GUY IN 1ST PLACE!!!

In the last year, I was in a finals where I thought the guy in 1st was
playing too conservatively (slowly) to allow anything to happen other
than [he wins on time out]. Which, incidentally, I hate.

Another player, who was in 5th place, told me to calm down, and that
he would transfer out if time was going to run out, just to stop the
player in 1st place from having the incentive to time the table out.
Which I thought was beautiful, cause he wouldn't lose anything, and
had much to gain.

> These kind of things have happened. Do happen. Will continue to happen.

And if these things keep players from "dragging their feet into
victory lane", then I hope they increase in frequency. In fact, I
will go this far:

ATTENTION PLAYERS:
If you're the 5th place finalist, and the player in 1st place has been
playing too slowly, TRANSFER YOURSELF OUT at 2 minutes. Don't let
stalling be a part of anyone's strategy.

> And with play-to-win assumed in the finals and some level of confusion (at
> least on my part) as to what level of losing-in-the-way-you-wish is
> allowed will continue to be "allowed".
>
> I am glad that we are having a serious discussion of possible
> modifications to the V:TES finals in order to ensure these kind of
> disgusting things are disallowed by the rules, since no one in these
> playgroups and/or tournaments has any courage to stand-up to their
> playmates and STOP this rotten behavior.

Slow play in the finals by whoever's in the lead is pretty rotten
behavior, which somehow hasn't been addressed by the rules yet. I
would endorse the previous rotten behavior, in order to curb this one.

----------

Now, I think almost all players AND judges, LSJ included, want the
game's final standings to be decided primarily by card play. Not by
talk, not by the timer, and not by random play. But I think mature
players will choose not to play very randomly anyway, so I think
that's not as big a concern as the other two are. I think table-
splitting for the win and time outs are two methods players use to
affect the finals standings, regularly, and that previous efforts to
rein them in have been largely unsuccessful. I believe that going to
1st place, 4 also-rans would likely affect these behaviors
significantly while the game gives up nothing.

Also, Kevin, I noticed that you said you wanted finals and prelims to
have the same time limit, for consistency. I think everyone wants
consistency, but your ideal final + prelim match in their real-time
length, while my ideal rounds match in number of turns taken. In
theory, there should be no difference between the length of a player's
turn between rounds, but in practice, somehow there seems to be a huge
difference. And so long as that's the case, finals should be extended
to afford all players the opportunity to play a game of the same
"length" as they would have played in any preliminary round.

Which should, IMO, be determined by asking, "When do 80% of tables
time out, for this group of players?" and setting the time limit to be
2hrs or that number, whichever is more.

-- Brian

> Good point Matt, but I would add, that with 30 seconds to go, after
> flinging yourself at your prey, knowing you will not get another turn,
> and still wanting to spike the 1st place seed's proverbial wheel, then
> transfer out.

Why is the 5th seed player waiting until 1:59:30 to try this tactic? At
1:15, the 5th seed guy should say to himself "this is going nowhere, I
need to make things happen." If you can't kill or get yourself killed in
45 minutes...well, nothing. You can.

This should spark a chain reaction of events that will ultimately lead to
the game ending one way or the other. If it's clear that your lunge isn't
going to get anywhere and you're just going to get yourself killed, the
top seed guy will realize he has to actually oust someone to win. Or
maybe he'll start calling Con Boons for you. Wow, 10 pool? Thanks. Now
I can buy two more Assault Rifles! Yeah, just spend it and keep going.

When a game goes to time with nobody ousted, it's because everybody waited
until the last 30 seconds to try to oust. That may be cunning play when
you're 1st seed, but it's stupid when you're 5th.

In other words, there's really no reason to ever do as you suggest. If
you sat there for an hour and 59 minutes doing nothing, then you might as
well let the top seed guy win. At least he worked for it in the
preliminary rounds. You and the other finalists chose to just sit for two
hours.

Matt Morgan

Messages.Body:
On Oct 11, 2:33 pm, "Kevin M." <youw...@imaspammer.org> wrote:


Its being taken out of context a bit.
If I feel someone is playing slowly a judge may or may not agree. I
would
of course first call a judge and ask. But I think we all know as
players that
this game can be played relatively slowly without being obvious about
it.

If as the game grinds towards time, I feel that a certain player
has held up the game in order to win on a time-out, and a judge when
consulted either disagrees or has added an insignificant amount of
time,
and I have not opted to agressively lunge 40 minutes ago as Matt
suggests for
whatever reason, and I entered the final in fifth place (thus having
nothing to lose), and on what I feel will be my last turn I have
lunged
forward in all out agression and failed to oust my prey, and I don't
think that
even if I got another turn I still would not be able to oust my prey,
and I'm in
a bad mood cause I did not sleep well the night before (or cause the
game's like
really gone to hell and back), I reserve the right to be spiteful and
oust myself
in the permitted fasion, assuming I feel my predator deserves it more
than
the first place player (cause they were not aiming for time).

It is not something I would do if the game is moving along.
It is not something I would do if somebody had already picked up a VP.

Its not corrupting the game, its King making. Which is an accepted
part of
the game at this point. Its not great kingmaking cause I can only make
my predator king. Will it teach them a lesson? Probably not, maybe if
I
explain it, but still probably not. Might make me feel better though.

Which do you think a new player would find more distasteful? Being
able to affect
the outcome of the game to the very end, or a game going to time
through
the actions of one player? Neither is very attractive but I would
rather
have an effect on the game. I suppose to be sporting I could warn the
table
with a few rounds to go that I might oust myself if no one else has
managed
a VP before time. As someone mentioned above this should get the table
moving,
but a threat is only good if everyone believes you will follow
through, and that
might not happen until the second time the above conditions are met.

I've seen some deplorable tactics employed in this game. Not often,
but there
have been some. All permitted by the rules. I find this less
distasteful than
the alternative of doing nothing.

I am fortunate enough that I don't get to finals tables very often.
And when I
do there is rarely a table going to time, perhaps because I do not run
into a lot of assholes playing VTES. Or because I manage to be ousted
before
the table goes to time. But I think this is what I would do if given
more
opportunity.

John P.
